title: Odawa raid at Eskippakithiki, 1753
summary: In January 1753 an Odawa raiding party struck John Finley’s trading post at Eskippakithiki in Clark County, Kentucky’s last major Native town of the 1700s.
bodyMarkdown:
[Eskippakithiki](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/596) was a Shawnee town in what is now Clark County. Its name meant "place of blue licks." Founded around 1718, it was a palisaded village of about 200 families who grew corn. Its origins are uncertain, and historians have offered several theories about where its founders came from.

## A trader's post

In the fall of 1752 the Pennsylvania trader [John Finley](/stories/john-finley-the-trader-who-put-kentucky-on-boones-map/) arrived at the Shawnees' invitation. He came with four servants and built a stockaded house and store.

## The January 1753 raid

On January 28, 1753, [a party of about 70 Conewago and Ottawa (Odawa) men](https://filsonhistorical.org/wp-content/uploads/publicationpdfs/6-4-2_Eskippakithiki-The-Last-Indian-Town-in-Kentucky_Beckner-Lucien.pdf), with a French Canadian and a Dutchman named Philip Philips, came south from the St. Lawrence. They were on an expedition against Southern Indian nations. In present Estill County they captured a group of Pennsylvania traders.

At Eskippakithiki the party clashed with Finley. Three of his servants were killed and all of his goods were seized. A trader's report sent east that winter also said three of Finley's men had been killed. Finley and his remaining servant, John Faulkner, fled through the winter woods to Pennsylvania.

The report of the raid sent to Pennsylvania officials used the place name "Kentucky." It is perhaps the earliest record of the word in the colonial papers.

## Abandonment

The Shawnee left Eskippakithiki soon afterward. One account suggests the Ottawa attack may have prompted the move. Another ties the departure to 1754, after the fall of Fort Necessity opened the French and Indian War, when the people joined kin in the Scioto Valley of southern Ohio. [Some histories](https://grokipedia.com/page/eskippakithiki) simply date the abandonment to about 1754–55. The father of the Shawnee leader Tecumseh lived at Eskippakithiki for part of his life.

## Kentucky today

A state historical marker calls the site the last of the Kentucky Indian towns. It describes the town, sometimes called "Kentake," as a meeting place for traders and Native hunters. Finley later met Daniel Boone in Braddock's army and [told him about the lands](https://grokipedia.com/page/john_finley_%28frontiersman%29) beyond the Cumberland Gap. The Clark County marker notes that Boone viewed the area on June 7, 1769.
